title: Crabgrass Catholicism and the Suburbanization of Catholics
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Suburban migration fundamentally transformed American Catholicism. Before WWII, Catholics concentrated in urban ethnic enclaves with parish-based community networks. Postwar suburbanization broke these ethnic-parish bonds, shifting identity from ethnicity to religion alone and replacing extended family networks with nuclear family isolation. The shift from Irish Catholic cultural dominance to Irish-style American Catholicism unified disparate ethnic traditions but fractured the thick community that sustained them.
points: Suburban migration dissolved ethnic-parish Catholic communities
Identity shifted from ethnic Catholicism to religious Catholicism
Extended family networks replaced by isolated nuclear families in suburbs
Irish Catholic style became dominant over other ethnic Catholic traditions
Suburbanization unified but weakened communal bonds sustaining American Catholicism
quotes: Postwar suburbanization helped complete the amalgamation of various ethnically inflected forms of Catholicism into one religiously identified body of American Catholicism.

In an era of rapid urbanization Catholic immigrants built American city life by fusing the neighborhood with the ethnic parish which was dominated by its priests and religious sisters, centered on its church and school, and bound together by its communal worship and devotions.

The suburbs were also comprised of single-family houses in which, especially in the earliest days of suburban development, a single generation of young veterans lived with their wives and children cut off from the extended family networks that long held the ethnic parish together.” Archived from The Hedgehog Review on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
